posts.title: Spring repotting week
posts.excerpt: Every March we lift about forty trees in one week, just as the buds swell. A note on what we look for when the roots come out.
posts.content:
Every March we lift about forty trees in one week, just as the buds swell. A note on what we look for when the roots come out.

Reading the roots

Healthy roots are pale and fine at the tips. A pot full of dark, circling roots means the tree has waited too long.

We comb out about a third, cut the thickest back to the trunk and keep every fine root we can.

Fresh soil

Our mix is two parts akadama, one pumice, one lava, sieved twice so water runs straight through.

A tree repotted on time hardly notices. A tree repotted late sulks for a year.

Haruo Kanzaki

posts.title: A forty-year juniper
posts.excerpt: The oldest juniper on the slope came as a cutting in 1986. It has had three pots, two keepers and one very bad winter.
posts.content:
The oldest juniper on the slope came as a cutting in 1986. It has had three pots, two keepers and one very bad winter.

The cutting

Haruo took it from a hedge behind the old carpenter’s house: a finger-length shoot, pushed into sand under a jam jar.

It spent eleven years in the ground before it was lifted, which is why the trunk is as thick as a wrist.

The deadwood

The silver stripe along the trunk is from the winter of 1998, when a branch split under snow. We kept it, and it is now the best part of the tree.

posts.title: First wiring
posts.excerpt: A first wiring lesson, written for the Saturday class: how thick, which way round and when to take it off.
posts.content:
A first wiring lesson, written for the Saturday class: how thick, which way round and when to take it off.

How thick

The wire should be about a third as thick as the branch. Too thin and it will not hold; too thick and it bruises.

Wrap at about forty-five degrees, anchored on the trunk or on a second branch, and never cross two wires.

When to take it off

Before it bites. On a growing maple that can be six weeks; on a juniper in winter, a season.

posts.title: Summer watering rounds
posts.excerpt: In July and August the slope is watered twice a day, first at six and again in the late afternoon. The rule is still the same.
posts.content:
In July and August the slope is watered twice a day, first at six and again in the late afternoon. The rule is still the same.

Look before you pour

Water when the surface turns pale and the pot feels light. Small pots dry first; we water them last so they get the coolest water.

Shade

From mid-July the shade cloth goes up over the maples and azaleas between noon and four.

posts.title: The maples in October
posts.excerpt: A short note from the upper beds, where the mountain maples are beginning to turn.
posts.content:
A short note from the upper beds, where the mountain maples are beginning to turn.

A slow turn

The maples go yellow at the tips first, then orange, then a deep red that lasts about ten days if the nights stay cold and dry.

We stop feeding in September so the leaves can harden and colour.

Open weekends

October and November weekends are the busiest on the slope. Come early; the light on the benches is best before ten.

posts.title: Moss and the gravel path
posts.excerpt: Why there is a tray of moss under every cedar on the slope, and what it does after repotting.
posts.content:
Why there is a tray of moss under every cedar on the slope, and what it does after repotting.

Growing moss

We scrape thin cushions from the gravel path and grow them on in shallow trays under the cedars, where it is cool and damp.

After repotting, a few pieces pressed onto fresh soil keep it from washing out and drying in the wind.

Not too much

Moss on the trunk holds water against the bark. Keep it to the soil.

products.description:
A compact shimpaku with a twisting trunk and a strip of silver deadwood, grown from a cutting at the nursery.

Kept in the ground for nine years to thicken the trunk, then lifted, first wired at fourteen and potted at sixteen. Full sun, outdoors all year.

products.description:
A fine-branched mountain maple that turns from spring green to deep red in late October.

Grown from seed in the upper beds. Leaves are reduced by pinching each June; the winter silhouette is as good as the leaves.

products.description:
A strong black pine with a slow, leaning trunk and dense pads of dark needles.

The most patient tree on the slope: decandled each summer, needles thinned each autumn. A tree to keep for a lifetime.

Age: 24 years · Height: 41 cm · Pot: Unglazed rectangle, 30 cm · Care level: Experienced care. Sent midweek, packed upright, with a handwritten care sheet.

products.description:
A low, spreading satsuki that flowers in soft pink each June, after the cherries and before the rain.

Satsuki grow in acid soil (kanuma), not ordinary bonsai mix. Repot and prune straight after flowering.
